summary: Gives best practices for using SIP to set up confidential media sessions. The SIP security toolbox has grown over the years but no single place explains how to combine it, and some mechanisms have feature gaps. This best current practice document pulls the guidance together and identifies those gaps.

plainLanguage.summary: Making a private phone call over the Internet can be done with several tools, and it's easy to get it wrong. This document is a how-to guide that says how to use them so nobody else can listen.

subtitle: How to set up encrypted SIP calls whose keys are tied to the caller's signed identity.

tldr.problem: SIP has many security tools, but nothing explains how to combine them so that call media is really encrypted and the encryption keys cannot be swapped by someone on the path.
tldr.mechanism: The SIPBRANDY profile of STIR has each endpoint sign the DTLS-SRTP key fingerprints in its SDP with an Identity header marked "msec", and requires DTLS-SRTP, ICE and STUN consent freshness.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice for comprehensive media confidentiality. It covers only comprehensive protection, not opportunistic security, and it cannot stop a legitimate endpoint from passing media on.

today: RFC 8862 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 228), published in January 2021, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 8224 and RFC 8225.

sections.title: Why a Best Practice Is Needed
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) comes with security services such as Digest Authentication, TLS for transport security and optionally S/MIME for body security. SIP often sets up audio or video sessions, which have their own protection such as the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP). Binding the security at the media layer to the security at the SIP layer relies on many external mechanisms, and this document explains their best use.

The motivation is pervasive monitoring. Opportunistic encryption tries to negotiate encryption and falls back to cleartext if that fails, and it typically has no integrity protection for the keying material. This document instead defines the SIPBRANDY profile (SIP Best-practice Recommendations Against Network Dangers to privacY) of STIR, which protects the keying material and gives application-layer assurance that media confidentiality is in place.
sections.plainLanguage: Plain locks on phone calls can be skipped if something goes wrong. This guide shows a stronger way, where both sides can prove the lock is really there.

sections.title: Comprehensive Protection Across SIP, SDP and RTP
sections.content:
There are two ways to protect media set up with SIP: comprehensive protection and opportunistic security. This document addresses only comprehensive protection. It needs three protocols working together: SIP, the Session Description Protocol (SDP) and the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP), in particular its secure profile SRTP.

SIP provides integrity protection for the media keying attributes carried in SDP, and those attributes identify the keys the endpoints use for the RTP media. The SDP k= line, which would need confidentiality in the signaling layer, MUST NOT be used with this profile.

Identity comes from STIR. Its Identity header carries a signature over request fields such as the From header field and over the media keys in SDP. As currently defined, STIR signs the a=fingerprint attribute, which is a fingerprint of the key used by DTLS-SRTP. So STIR gives comprehensive protection only when DTLS-SRTP is the media security service, although the PASSporT token it uses is extensible to other SDP attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: Three helpers pass the secret together. One sets up the call, one describes it, and one carries the voices. The first one signs the lock details so nobody can swap them.

sections.title: The SIPBRANDY Profile of STIR
sections.content:
In the SIPBRANDY profile, the STIR verification service works together with the SRTP media endpoint, to make sure the key fingerprints in SDP match the keys exchanged for DTLS-SRTP. That is why the verification service function sits in the SIP User Agent Server, composed with the media endpoint. An intermediary doing the signing or verifying could act as a man in the middle and alter fingerprints, and STIR offers no protection against that because its core threat model is impersonation.

So the profile shifts responsibility to the endpoints. Intermediaries MAY verify, but verification must be repeated at the endpoint, and intermediaries MUST NOT block or redirect calls just because they do not trust the signing credential. User agents MUST implement both the authentication service and verification service roles of RFC 8224, MUST signal compliance by adding the msec claim to the PASSporT payload, and MUST include an a=fingerprint attribute in every offer and answer.

The profile is built on an end-to-end trust model: endpoints, not intermediaries, decide whether to accept a signing credential.
sections.plainLanguage: The two people on the call check each other's ID themselves. They do not trust a helper in the middle to do it for them.

sections.title: Credentials and Anonymous Calls
sections.content:
An endpoint needs a credential to sign for its identity, which is usually a SIP URI or a telephone number in the From header field. The RFC notes that few commercial certification authorities issue certificates for SIP URIs or telephone numbers, and work on systems for this is not yet mature enough to recommend. Without such certificates, DTLS-SRTP permits self-signed public keys, and SIPBRANDY uses the relaxed authority rules of RFC 8224 to allow them, with a subject matching the user's identity. A self-signed certificate needs some out-of-band verification for comprehensive protection, and could support trust on first use. Relying parties SHOULD NOT use revocation checks or real-time certificate verification for self-signed certificates.

For anonymous calls, the identity anonymous@anonymous.invalid cannot be signed under RFC 8224, but a valid domain such as anonymous@example.com can. One-time self-signed certificates SHOULD include a subjectAltName of sip:anonymous@anonymous.invalid, SHOULD be discarded after the session, and a new one SHOULD be generated before each later anonymous call. A man in the middle can still strip the Identity header and sign its own, so this signature only protects against entities that modify SDP without being Identity-aware.
sections.plainLanguage: If you do not have an official ID card, you can make your own, but then you should also tell the other person in another way. For secret calls you make a fresh one-use card each time.

sections.title: Connected Identity and Authorization Decisions
sections.content:
STIR protects fingerprints in SIP requests but not in SIP responses, so a secured SDP body going back to the caller cannot be carried in a 200-class response. It requires an extra round trip, typically a request sent in the backwards direction. RFC 4916 (connected identity) does this with an UPDATE request, and the profile adds conditions: the UPDATE carrying signed SDP with a fingerprint must be sent during dialog establishment after the PRACK that follows a provisional 1xx response, and the UAS must act as an authentication service for that UPDATE.

On authorization, a verification service that receives a dialog-forming request with a PASSporT type of msec MUST reject it if validation fails. If it is valid and the terminating user accepts, that user MUST send its own signed request with an msec PASSporT, for end-to-end bidirectional confidentiality.

The msec type can be a mandatory or a merely opportunistic request. If no signed request comes back, the UA either shuts down the dialog, when policy requires msec support, or, if policy permits (for example explicit user acceptance), lets the dialog continue without media security.
sections.plainLanguage: When you call someone, they have to answer with their own signed proof too. If they cannot, you either hang up or knowingly keep talking without the lock.

sections.title: Media Security Protocols
sections.content:
SDP can negotiate media security in several ways. RFC 8643 considers DTLS-SRTP, security descriptions and ZRTP for the opportunistic case. For this specification, support for DTLS-SRTP is REQUIRED.

The mky claim of PASSporT gives integrity protection for a=fingerprint attributes in SDP, including when several such attributes appear in the same SDP.
sections.plainLanguage: There are several kinds of locks for voice calls. This guide picks one kind that every phone must be able to use.

sections.title: Relayed Media and Conferencing
sections.content:
Media relays complicate end-to-end confidentiality. Many just proxy media, but others present themselves as media endpoints and end the security association before re-originating the media. Centralized conference bridges typically do this to mix media from several sources, so often only hop-by-hop confidentiality is possible. Work on combining hop-by-hop and end-to-end encryption is described as not mature enough to become a best practice.

Back-to-Back User Agents (B2BUAs) that follow the guidance of RFC 7879 may relay media while still allowing end-to-end confidentiality. Finally, if an endpoint can decrypt media, it can forward the decrypted media without the originator's knowledge or consent, and no media confidentiality mechanism can prevent that.
sections.plainLanguage: If a helper in the middle opens the box to mix voices together, the lock only protects each separate hop. And anyone who legitimately hears the call can always repeat it to someone else.

sections.title: ICE, Consent and the Resulting Requirements
sections.content:
Implementations MUST support Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) to enable end-to-end connectivity and avoid media relays, and it is RECOMMENDED that they support Trickle ICE to speed up call setup. With connected identity, the answer carrying the key fingerprints and STIR signature arrives in an UPDATE, a provisional response and a PRACK, so the media keys count as exchanged only when that UPDATE is received. To limit the denial-of-service attack described in RFC 8445, implementations MUST implement the STUN usage for consent freshness from RFC 7675.

The best practices for SIP UAs are summarized as four MUST-level requirements: support the SIPBRANDY profile and signal it with msec, follow the authorization decision behavior, support DTLS-SRTP for key management, and support ICE and STUN consent freshness.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending voices, the phones check that the other side really wants them. And the phone should only show a lock symbol once the keys have truly been swapped.

messages.label: UPDATE + Identity (msec)
messages.note: Signed SDP with the callee's fingerprint.

items.title: SIPBRANDY
items.text: Support the profile and signal it with msec in PASSporT.

items.title: Authorization
items.text: Follow the decision behavior of Section 4.4.

items.title: ICE and consent
items.text: Support ICE and STUN consent freshness.
